issues.title: Add helpers for reading/writing to physical memory with QEMU
issues.body:
You can read from a physical address with QEMU using: `monitor xp <phy_addr>`

But I don't see any way to write to a physical address. It seems like there's a way to convert all reads/writes to physical ones using [this](https://qemu-project.gitlab.io/qemu/system/gdb.html#examining-physical-memory):
```
> maintenance packet qqemu.PhyMemMode
This will return either 0 or 1, 1 indicates you are currently in the physical memory mode.

> maintenance packet Qqemu.PhyMemMode:1
This will change the memory mode to physical memory.

> maintenance packet Qqemu.PhyMemMode:0
This will change it back to normal memory mode.
```

It would be useful to have some helpers to either directly work with these commands (i.e. `qemu_mem_mode [phys|virt]`), or override the `set` builtin to take a `-phys` argument that will use these maintenance commands to do physical writes.

The first option will be easier to implement, although the second would be more ergonomic. I'm fine with either in the short-term.

issues.title: Enable skipped tests on aarch64 by making them architecture-agnostic (x86-64 & aarch64)
issues.body:
A large number of tests under `tests/library/dbg/tests/` are currently marked as `SKIPPED` when running the test suite on `aarch64`. These tests pass on `x86-64`, but their current implementation relies on x86-specific assumptions (e.g. registers, ABI details, instruction layout, or heap internals), which prevents them from running on aarch64.

The goal of this task is to rewrite or refactor these tests so that they are architecture-agnostic and can be executed on both x86-64 and aarch64, without unconditional `pytest.skip` based on the architecture.


### Scope of work
- The work does **not** need to be completed in a single pull request — individual tests or small groups of tests can be refactored independently and submitted as separate PRs, allowing multiple contributors to work in parallel.
- Identify and remove x86-64–specific assumptions in the affected tests (e.g. register names, instruction encodings, ABI- or heap-layout details).
- Refactor tests to rely on pwndbg architecture abstractions where available.
- Use test parameterization or architecture-aware helpers instead of unconditional `pytest.skip`.
- Replace architecture-dependent assertions with conditional assertions when behavior is expected to differ.
- Keep `pytest.skip` only for cases where a feature is genuinely unavailable on a given architecture.

### Acceptance criteria

- At least one previously skipped test is made to run successfully on aarch64 without breaking x86-64 support.
- Refactored tests are no longer marked as **SKIPPED** on aarch64.
- The test suite continues to pass on:
  - x86-64
  - aarch64
- No regressions are introduced for existing x86-64 test coverage.
- Tests remain readable, maintainable, and consistent with existing pwndbg test patterns.

issues.title: Cache remote file fetches
issues.body:
A handful of Pwndbg commands require access to the file being debugged, such as to extract ELF information. When debugging remotely, we use the underlying debuggers "remote file fetch" capability to get these files. Currently, the file fetch is not cached, and is put into a temporary directory here https://github.com/pwndbg/pwndbg/blob/0c51d56dc41babc13161a94dc24290fd40b3b52c/pwndbg/aglib/file.py#L102-L108

This results in the file being fetched multiple times, even for the same debugging instance. These file fetches should be cached, at least for a given debugging run, and perhaps even between runs.

issues.title: Add command for breaking on a particular call chain
issues.body:
Sometimes I want to set a breakpoint on the function `c()`, but only if we reached there first from a call to `a()`, followed by a call to `b()`. That is, the call chain (or reverse stack trace) would be `a()` -> ... -> `b()` -> ... -> `c()`. If we reached `c()` through a chain like `d()` -> `b()` -> `c()`, we shouldn't hit the breakpoint.

The command could be something like `bchain` (breakpoint for a call chain), and it would take a list of breakpoint addresses, i.e. `bchain a b c`, and it could also include instruction addresses as well (preferably accepting both the `*` and no `*` syntax).

For the implementation, I think the way it would work would be: set a normal breakpoint on the first breakpoint in the chain (i.e. `a`) with some commands that would executed when the breakpoint is hit. These commands would run `tbreak` (temporary breakpoint) on the next breakpoint address and then continue. The next breakpoints will repeat this process until we hit the final breakpoint (i.e. `c`), in which case no commands will execute.

We would also need to have finish breakpoints in each function, so that we could clean up a breakpoint that was set but never hit during that execution of the function.

issues.title: Unicorn Emulation: Disassemble after loops
issues.body:
If we hit a `rep stosd` or similar, we stop disassembling because we loop back to the same instruction over and over, and we hit the emulation limit.

We should have a special case that if an instruction is followed (per Unicorn) by itself, that we start disassembling instructions starting at the next instruction.  This will break emulation, since the next instruction may be a `cmp` followed by a `jnz` and we won't be able to follow it... but it'll be better than a blind loop where the disassembly magically just "stops".

issues.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Not sure how common this is in general buf or me on aarch64 inside PLT entries, functions are "branched" into (with a `br`) instruction rather than called into (`bl`). The x86_64 equivalents would be jmp and call. When this happens, pwndbg doesn't show function arguments. This makes sense in the general case because we want to avoid false-positives like showing arguments on if-statement branches etc.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
That being said, we could do a check like "is the destination of this branch a function (symbol)". That way we would avoid any false-positives and nicely cover this edge case.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Special case PLT entries somehow in case:

issues.title: nextproginstr fails if the next program instruction is higher up on the callstack
issues.body:
`nextproginstr` works by continuously finding the next `ret` instruction, going to it, and stepping forwards. The idea is that you are popping stack frames off the stack until you get back to code belonging to the binary itself.

The assumption is that your code calls into external libraries, such as libc, and you might find yourself deeply nested inside the library functions, and you want to return back to the binaries code.

However, when you `starti` a program, such as one dynamically linked against libc, you start at an address within the loaders address space. Your program code will start much later, higher up in the call stack. `nextproginstr` does not work in this case, but it would be nice if it did.

Perhaps there could be a flag, like `nextproginstr --up`, then tells it that your code is going to be higher up in the call stack, so it should be looking to step into call instructions in order to find your code.

Or, this functionality may not be needed (just do `b main`), but it should be documented in the help command.

issues.title: don't do backwards linear disassembly in the context when stepping
issues.body:
We don't want to show the linear backwards disassembly in the disassembly context when we step into a function (because those are just the instructions from the previous function, and they clutter the output).

We want to show backwards linear disassembly only when we continued the process in some way `e.g. pwndbg> continue` or `pwndbg> nexti`, and hit a stop because of that command (e.g. pressed Ctrl-C, hit a breakpoint, caught a signal).

I don't really see a way in the gdb python docs to make this differentiation though: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Events-In-Python.html#Events-In-Python . GDB seems to simply not expose enough event info.

Maybe we could leverage this: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Hooks.html . But seems flaky.

Side-note: possibly with `nearpc` we want to do backwards disassembly in more cases than in the disassembly context.

issues.title: make gdb event handling aware of passed information
issues.body:
When GDB triggers an event, the only information that we keep track of is which event it was. But this is bad, since a lot of other information is also passed which is not easily available through other means.

https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Events-In-Python.html

### Example 1 - call info

https://github.com/pwndbg/pwndbg/pull/3813#issuecomment-4042298727

We lose information on whether an `events.inferior_call` is a `gdb.InferiorCallPreEvent` or `gdb.InferiorCallPostEvent` which is important for cache clearing.

### Example 2 - signals

We triggered a GDB crash (https://sourceware.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=34047) because we ran `info program` during an exit event. We do this, because we are oblivious to when a signal event actually happens.

But we could easily fix this if we were more event-aware, because a `gdb.StopEvent` can be a `gdb.SignalEvent` which has the signal information. And clearly this is the intended way to catch this.
